title: A Settling or Tilting House: Signs, Causes and Remedies
desc: Spot a settling or tilting house early via cracks, jammed doors and sunken floors; common causes, foundation remedies and what owners must do if it is unsafe.
summary: Signs of a settling or tilting house, common causes, technical remedies and legal responsibilities when a house risks becoming unsafe or settles because of a neighbouring building.
body: p

Some settlement is normal in every building in its early stage, but uneven settlement or prolonged settlement is the problem: cracked walls, tilting, jammed doors and broken pipes. Early detection makes remedies cheaper and safer.
h2
1. Signs that a house is settling or tilting
ul
Diagonal cracks in walls, especially around doors and on lower floors, tending to widen.
Doors and windows suddenly jam, with uneven gaps at the top and bottom.
Floors crack or sink, floor tiles lift or bulge; the house sits lower compared with the road or yard.
The gap between your house and the neighbouring house opens wider, or the two houses lean on each other.
By eye or with a plumb line, walls and columns are no longer vertical.
Underground water pipes or the septic tank break or leak for no clear reason.
h2
2. Common causes
ol
Soft ground (pond, filled paddy, muddy soil) without a geological survey, with an unsuitable foundation chosen.
A foundation on non-uniform ground: partly on hard soil and partly on fill.
Added load: adding floors, extensions, placing water tanks or heavy materials without checking the foundation.
Impact from neighbouring works: deep foundation excavation, lowering groundwater, driving piles, vibration during construction.
Water weakening the ground: water supply and drainage pipes leaking for a long time, waterlogging under the foundation.
h2
3. What to do immediately
p

Under Clause 1, Article 42 of Decree 207/2026/ND-CP, when a building risks becoming unsafe, the owner is responsible for re-checking its condition, arranging a quality inspection (if needed), applying emergency measures such as restricting or stopping use, cordoning off the danger zone, moving people and property if collapse is possible, and reporting immediately to the nearest local authority. In practice, you should:
ul
Mark, measure and photograph the cracks by date to track how fast they develop.
Have a structural engineer or an inspection organisation survey; settlement monitoring or an additional geological survey may be needed.
Check and immediately repair any leaking pipes around the foundation.
Temporarily reduce load: do not store heavy items on upper floors, and stop extensions.
h2
4. Technical remedies
p

Depending on the cause and severity, an engineer may propose: strengthening or widening the foundation; adding piles beneath the existing foundation; treating and improving the ground; reducing the building load; in the case of tilting, straightening may be possible – this is complex, high-risk work that only an experienced firm should undertake. Only after the foundation has been treated and settlement has stabilised should cracks be repaired and finishes completed; repairing cracks while the house is still settling will lead to cracking again.
p

Strengthening foundations and structure affects the load-bearing structure, so it usually does not fall within the permit exemption for repair and renovation under Point h, Clause 2, Article 43 of the Construction Law 2025; ask the local permit-issuing authority before carrying out the work.
h2
5. Settlement caused by a neighbour's construction: who is responsible?
p

If settlement or cracks appear while the adjoining house is under construction, prepare a condition record confirmed by the parties and the authorities, require the work causing the impact to be suspended and request compensation. For details see the article building causes a neighbour's house to settle or crack: liability and compensation and how construction incidents are handled. When building a new house yourself on soft ground, investing in a geological survey and the right foundation design from the start is always much cheaper than dealing with settlement later.
p

note

This article is for reference; diagnosing the cause of settlement and the foundation remedy must be done by a structural or geotechnical engineer or an inspection organisation after an actual survey. The rules cited are from Construction Law 135/2025/QH15 and Decree 207/2026/ND-CP (in force).
